title: I'm not a programmer, but I designed a multiplayer space 4X and built it with Claude Code over about eight weeks. Here's how we split the work.
author: SovereignFlip
selftext:
I've played strategy games my whole life, but I've never written code. About eight weeks ago I started building \*\*Star Sovereign\*\*, a free browser space 4X based on a game I loved in the early 2000s called Web Space Alliance. It runs on PC and phones, with no ads and no download. I wanted to share how the process actually worked, because it ended up very different from what I expected.

**My job was the game itself:** I came up with every rule, how the planets and ships work, the four AI species and how each one should behave, the story, and all the balance decisions. I'd describe an idea in plain English, often a rough one, and Claude would ask questions or suggest how it could work for each species and from the player's point of view. Then I'd say yes or no. One thing I learned early: Claude sometimes builds a "better" version of what you asked for. So I set a rule that it can always suggest a better idea and explain why, but it builds my version unless I agree to the change. That one rule saved a lot of frustration.

It worked the other way too. Plenty of times Claude got stuck on a problem and kept trying fixes that didn't work. I started asking it to explain the problem to me in plain words, along with everything it had already tried, and more than once my idea was the one that fixed it. You don't need to know how to code to spot that something is being solved the wrong way.

**Claude's job was the code, all of it**: the browser client, the server, multiplayer turns, the bots, the tutorial, push alerts for phones, and the release process. I was also completely new to Linux when I started, so it walked me through setting up my PC as well. It keeps memory notes of every decision and every correction I give it, so when I tell it "don't do that again," it actually doesn't. By the end there were dozens of these notes, things like "never slow down the early game" and "show me new screens before you release them."

Testing was shared, and it was the part that surprised me most. At first we balanced the game by running thousands of bot-vs-bot simulations, and the numbers looked fine. But when I played, the game felt wrong. So we changed approach: Claude started playing full games as a human player against the bots, under fair rules (it only sees what a player would see, with no peeking at the database). Afterwards it writes up what was broken, unfair, or exploitable. It also keeps a list of lessons from every game it plays and re-reads it before the next one. Those play-throughs found far more real problems than the simulations did.

Humans still caught what the AI missed. My friends Rohan and Skyler played early builds. Once, a tutorial bug got past all of Claude's testing and stopped them at mission 14. Watching a real new player is still the best test there is. 

All the art is hand-drawn by Alyson: [https://www.instagram.com/alyson\_the\_lord](https://www.instagram.com/alyson_the_lord), and my friend Cameron Lockhart hosts the game on his server.

**On cost:** I did all of this on the Pro plan. I use the bigger model for design talks and bug hunts, and hand the clear, already-decided building steps to the smaller one to make my usage last longer.

The game has been live for a small group since mid-October, and I'm opening it up now:

Game: [https://play.starsovereigngame.com/?from=aigamedev](https://play.starsovereigngame.com/?from=aigamedev)

Discord: [https://discord.gg/7gY93Jfaa](https://discord.gg/7gY93Jfaa)

Happy to answer questions about any part of the workflow!
